Postal, Hatred, and Weighing the Worth of Asshole Simulators

An asshole simulator is lost on me. Most people in my life seem to think I'm an asshole as it is.

I'll stick to euro truck simulator :)

I watched the whole thing, all 1 hour and 25 minutes of it. It's actually quite a good representational history of the entire postal franchise, a franchise that centers around being as offensive and politically incorrect as possible. It is professionally written and expertly narrated.

For the considerable amount of time that is spent talking about the Postal franchise, that's not really what it's about. Instead, the postal franchise serves as the framework for a larger idea. The idea that violence and intentional offensiveness is simultaneously not that interesting when paired together in the absence of any other design objective, but also that it's a fine line to walk between being darkly satirical, and being just plain full of yourself.

The video continues onward to tie these ideas to the gamergate controversy, which is I feel the real subject the author wanted to discuss. He goes on to show how some of the extremes of gamergate are a bit ridiculous. Ridiculous in a way where I'd walk up to you and say something amazingly offensive to your face, and then add the catchall "no offense" as though that made it all ok.

I found myself genuinely torn between these ideas. On one hand I feel freedom of expression in a game is something that needs to be protected. On the other, it was hard not to see the points he was making. You can in fact go too far. Despite this, his message is not "don't make these games", it's more like "if you make games like this, don't be surprised if someone is offended. Don't be shocked if the game doesn't sell as well as you hoped it would. Don't accuse your customer base of not appreciating your vision because they were too stupid to understand it.".

I think this is really one of the most introspective and analytical gamer videos that I've seen in a long time. It doesn't attempt to polarize on one side or the other, and instead explores the changing attitudes to a niche genre through the eyes of one person as he gets older.
